<reason>Both sides were strong, disciplined, and format-compliant, but B built the sturdier path. A's opening leaned on characterizing the motion as a "public browse of everyone else's kin," which B credibly exposed as a strawman since tiered access and tribal authority were in B's case from the start. A's best surviving route — that only the state program can override a birth parent's or tribal nation's "no" ("non-compulsion") — was sharp and partially live, but B answered it comparatively: refusals only gain legal force through public law, firms never ask at all, and the motion never mandated opening sealed files. The decisive ground was findability. B's pressure question (who pays to make an unindexed record findable?) forced A's locator-service answer, which B then dismantled: a petition requiring name, place, and date serves only the already-documented, while the motion's core victims — renamed adoptees, numbered children, unrecorded sales — are exactly those a petition-first system never hears, and proving descent requires the surrounding archive ("kinship is a network"). A's closing reply ("a claim needs a claimant") was honest but functionally abandoned the worst-severed, and A's late "fee-waived search of the box" presupposed the indexing A opposed. B also narrowed the debate to a clean decision rule (default access vs petition) and read the motion more faithfully. B's clipped first rebuttal was a minor execution cost; the substance had landed.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2 and closing converting A's own "locatable right" into a concession: "a right to a file you cannot find is no right at all," capped by "their model serves the documented; ours finds the erased" — showing A's alternative presupposes B's digitization while abandoning the motion's core beneficiaries. A never squarely answered it.</best_rebuttal>
